chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:
I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the stoning (of the Jamarat), so he said: 'Do not stone the Jamarat unless you are in a state of purity.'
This is the most preferable (state), and if he stones them while not in a state of purity, there is no penalty upon him.

key_terms.الْأَفْضَلُ: The most preferable or recommended (mustahabb) action
key_terms.الْجِمَارِ: The Jamarat (pillars/stones) in Mina, used for the ritual of Rami al-Jamarat
key_terms.شَيْءٌ: Penalty or consequence (in this context, no sin or required compensation)
key_terms.طُورٍ: Ritual purity (Taharah), specifically referring to the state of being free from major or minor impurities

ai.seo_question: Is ritual purity required for stoning the Jamarat in Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the virtue of maintaining ritual purity (taharah) during the stoning of the Jamarat is highlighted as the preferred (afdhal) state, reflecting the general principle that acts of worship are enhanced by physical cleanliness. However, the Imam clarifies that impurity does not invalidate the pillar itself, distinguishing this act from prayer where impurity may be more restrictive. This ruling underscores the flexibility in Hajj rituals while encouraging believers to maximize spiritual merit through adherence to sunnah.
